claims.claim: The wind is coming from the Almada side, directly against the boat's heading
The boat crosses from one bank to the other under sail and oars
The boat beats (sails close-hauled) against the wind
Boats carried passengers between Lisbon and Almada
Navigation was done by sail and oars
Crossing from one bank of the river to the other was a Tagus route

lines.en: Wind's coming off Almada, right on our nose. We'll beat across under sail and oars, bank to bank. And you still haven't told me why you're going.
lines.pt: O vento vem de Almada, mesmo de frente. Vamos à bolina, à vela e a remos, de uma margem à outra. E a menina ainda não me disse ao que vai.

claims.claim: Boats carried passengers from Lisbon to Almada
The wind is ahead of the boat
The boat uses sail and oars as always
Boats carried passengers between Lisbon and Almada
Navigation was done by sail and oars

lines.en: Another passenger from Lisbon to Almada. Wind ahead, sail and oars as always. So tell me, miss, what takes you to the other bank?
lines.pt: Mais uma passageira de Lisboa para Almada. Vento de frente, vela e remos, como sempre. Diga lá, menina, o que a leva à outra margem?

claims.claim: Tacking means turning through the wind to change sides (the order to tack)
Sheeting in (caçar) follows the tack
Bringing the bow round through the wind makes the sails change sides (tacking)
The sail is sheeted in after the manoeuvre

lines.pt: Passa a proa, caça a vela!

claims.claim: You cannot sail straight into the wind; you tack, zigzagging from one side to the other
The river has fragatas and faluas on it and is full of traffic
Going upwind means tacking and zigzagging between two close-hauled headings
The river was busy with varied craft including fragatas and faluas

lines.en: "Why do we keep zigzagging?" "You can't sail straight into the wind, miss. We tack, one side then the other. Look at the fragatas and faluas: the river's full."
lines.pt: — Porque andamos aos ziguezagues? — Contra o vento não se vai a direito, menina. Vira-se de bordo, de um lado e do outro. Olhe as fragatas e as faluas: o rio está cheio.

claims.claim: You cannot go straight into the wind; you zigzag close-hauled on one tack then the other
A falua carries people
Going upwind means zigzagging between two close-hauled headings
Faluas also carried passengers

lines.en: "Can't we just go straight?" "Not into the wind. We zigzag, close-hauled on one side, then the other. That falua carries people too."
lines.pt: — E não podemos ir a direito? — Ao vento, não. Vai-se em ziguezague, à bolina de um bordo e do outro. Aquela falua também leva gente.

claims.claim: Bearing away, easing the sheet and letting the sail fill are the right manoeuvre/commands

lines.en: Bear away! Ease, let her fill!

claims.claim: Bear off, ease the sheet, then sheet in is the correct sequence

lines.en: Bear off, ease, then sheet in.

claims.claim: The river is the road between the banks
A boat was the fastest way to cross
The Tagus linked the two banks as a road
Boats were faster than other means

lines.en: "Why stay at this?" "The river's the road between the banks, and a boat's the fastest way." "I'm going to see my mother."
lines.pt: — Porque fica nisto? — O rio é a estrada entre as margens, e o barco o caminho mais rápido. — Vou ver a minha mãe.

claims.claim: The river joins the two banks
The river linked the two banks

lines.en: "Why not give this up?" "It's the river that joins the two banks, miss." "Then hurry: my brother marries today."
lines.pt: — Porque não larga isto? — É o rio que liga as duas margens, menina. — Então leve-me depressa: o meu irmão casa hoje.

claims.claim: Coming alongside is done gently, controlling speed
The boat arrives at Almada carrying passengers from Lisbon
Many people pass through the boat, each with their own reason
Coming alongside means controlling speed to berth at a quay
Boats carried passengers to Almada

lines.en: Easy now, you come alongside gently. There, Almada. So many people pass through this boat, each with their own reason. Go on, miss, and good luck.
lines.pt: Devagar, que se acosta com jeito. Pronto, Almada. Passa tanta gente por este barco, cada uma com a sua razão. Vá, menina, e boa sorte.

claims.claim: Taking the way off and easing to the quay is how you come alongside
The boatman carries people from Lisbon to Almada
The passenger paid with a coin
Coming alongside a quay involves controlling speed
Boats carried passengers between Lisbon and Almada

lines.en: Take her way off, ease to the quay... we're alongside. I carry people from Lisbon to Almada, each with their own story. Thanks for the coin, miss.
lines.pt: Tira-lhe o seguimento, encosta ao cais... acostámos. Levo gente de Lisboa a Almada, e cada um leva a sua história. Obrigado pela moeda, menina.

claims.claim: The catraio was a small Tagus boat carrying passengers
The caíque, bote, batel and canoa also carried passengers
River traffic linked the banks until the mid-20th century
Before the 1966 bridge, boats were the fastest way
The catraio was a small Tagus boat carrying passengers
Passenger transport used the catraio, caíque, bote, batel and canoa
River traffic linked the banks until the mid-20th century
Before the bridge, in 1966, boats were faster than other means

lines.en: My passenger and I are invented. But the catraio was real: a small Tagus boat carrying passengers, like the caíque, bote, batel and canoa. River traffic linked the banks until the mid-20th century, and before the bridge of 1966 boats were the fastest way.
lines.pt: Eu e a minha passageira somos inventados. Mas o catraio existiu: um pequeno barco do Tejo que levava passageiros, tal como o caíque, o bote, o batel e a canoa. O tráfego no rio ligou as margens até meados do século XX, e antes da ponte de 1966 os barcos eram o caminho mais rápido.

claims.claim: The catraio, falua and bote cacilheiro were well-known passenger boats
Until the mid-20th century the river carried people and goods between the banks
Before the 1966 bridge boats beat any other means
The catraio, falua and bote cacilheiro were well-known passenger boats
Until the mid-20th century river traffic carried people and goods between the banks
Before the bridge, in 1966, boats were faster than other means

lines.en: Tio Joaquim and the passenger are fiction. Real are the catraio and other well-known passenger boats, like the falua and bote cacilheiro. Until the mid-20th century the river carried people and goods between the banks, and before the 1966 bridge boats beat any other means.
lines.pt: O Tio Joaquim e a passageira são ficção. Verdadeiros são o catraio e outros barcos de passageiros conhecidos, como a falua e o bote cacilheiro. Até meados do século XX, o rio levou gente e mercadorias entre as margens, e antes da ponte de 1966 os barcos ganhavam a qualquer outro meio.
